org.name: EcoKheti Foundation
org.experience: Section 8 non-profit company registered in 2016 and working in Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh. It has 8 years in community-based livelihoods, 6 in maternal and child nutrition and 5 in climate-resilient livelihoods. Annual revenue is Rs 2.4 Crore, with 9 permanent staff and a 5-member board. Relevant track record: (1) an SRLM-funded SHG-led livelihoods and nutrition project with 1,200 women in Khunti and Gumla, which reported an income increase of at least 45% and improved dietary diversity in 60% of households; (2) a CSR-funded climate-resilient agriculture project with 800 farmers in Chhattisgarh, where 70% adopted climate-adaptive practices; (3) strengthening of 3 FPOs (900 members) in Jharkhand, which roughly doubled aggregated sales.
org.values: Community ownership, women's agency, convergence with public systems. No political or religious affiliation.

theme: Maternal and child nutrition through SHG-led nutrition-sensitive livelihoods and convergence with ICDS and health services (working title: Poshan Saathi: SHG-led Kitchen Gardens, Nutrition Counselling and ICDS Convergence for Mothers and Young Children in Murhu, Khunti)

geography.coverage: 20 villages in Murhu block. The villages are still to be named; they will be selected for existing SHG presence and Anganwadi centre catchments, and checked for overlap with JSLPS Didi Badi / FNHW coverage.

target: About 1,200 women from SHG member households with pregnant or lactating women and/or children under five, across 20 villages. How many of the 1,200 are currently pregnant or lactating, and the number of children under five, will be established at baseline and triangulated with Anganwadi registers.
budget: Rs 1,39,89,608 against an indicative ceiling of Rs 1.4 Crore (Rs 1,40,00,000) over 2 years. The ceiling is still to be confirmed.
problem_facts: SETTING: Khunti district had a population of 5,31,885 (Census 2011). 91.55% was rural, 73.25% was Scheduled Tribe and 4.52% Scheduled Caste. Forest covers about 40% of the district area. [Khunti district website, S1; Vikaspedia Aspirational Districts, S4]

MURHU BLOCK: The population was 85,486 and entirely rural, with 79.19% ST and 13,907 children aged 0–6 (Census 2011 PCA as compiled by a secondary source; to be verified against the DCHB). The number of villages and households is a gap to be filled from the DCHB. [S2]

COMMUNITY: Munda (83.66% of Khunti's ST population) and Oraon (8.52%) are the main tribal communities in the district (secondary compilation of Census 2011; to be verified). Murhu-specific tribal composition is a gap. [S3]

LOW FEMALE LITERACY: Female literacy is 53.69% in Khunti against 74.08% for males. Murhu figures are almost identical: 53.66% female and 73.15% male (secondary compilation). At state level, 32% of women aged 15–49 in Jharkhand have never attended school (NFHS-5). This supports pictorial, oral counselling for low-literacy audiences. [S1, S2, S6]

POVERTY: The BPL share in Khunti was 35.45% in 2011-12 (secondary source; the original government source is still to be located). Block-level livelihood, landholding, migration and PDS data are gaps; the baseline will capture household food security, land and water access, and migration. [S5]

UNDERNUTRITION BURDEN (STATE): In Jharkhand, 40% of children under five are stunted, 22% wasted, 9% severely wasted and 39% underweight (NFHS-5, 2019-21). The national figures are 35.5% stunted, 19.3% wasted and 32.1% underweight, so Jharkhand is worse on each. [S6, S10]
ANAEMIA: 67% of children in Jharkhand are anaemic (NFHS-5). Anaemia among women has not fallen since NFHS-4. [S7, S6]

DISTRICT SEVERITY: All 24 Jharkhand districts, Khunti included, are of public health concern on WHO thresholds for stunting, wasting, severe wasting and anaemia. Under NFHS-4, Khunti was among the districts with the highest shares of underweight and severely wasted children (secondary analysis). Khunti's NFHS-5 district values are a GAP and will be taken from the IIPS district fact sheet; project-area values will be established by the baseline survey. [S8, S9]

FEEDING PRACTICES: Only 22% of children aged 6–23 months in Jharkhand ate iron-rich foods in the previous day (NFHS-5). Minimum dietary diversity, minimum adequate diet and exclusive breastfeeding for Khunti and for target households will be established at baseline. [S6]

SERVICE UPTAKE GAP: Poshan 2.0 entitles families to supplementary nutrition (THR), nutrition and health education, immunisation, health check-ups and referral. Take-up in Murhu (AWC numbers, THR regularity, growth monitoring coverage, VHSND functioning, ANC and PMMVY uptake) is not documented and will be established at baseline and through a mapping of Anganwadi centres and health facilities. [S22]

WEAK SAM CONTINUUM: Jharkhand runs 88 Malnutrition Treatment Centres (MTCs) under NHM, and Anganwadi Workers detect severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in the community. A study found that 52% of children were still severely wasted and 83% underweight at the end of the community phase of the MTC programme. This points to weak follow-up after discharge. The nearest functional MTC for Murhu is a gap. [S12]

CAUSAL LOGIC: Immediate causes are poor dietary diversity and suboptimal feeding and care in pregnancy and the first 1,000 days. Underlying causes are limited year-round access to diverse foods, low awareness in low-literacy households, and incomplete take-up of ICDS and health entitlements. Structural causes are poverty, remoteness and the sex gap in literacy. State programmes exist (Didi Badi Yojana, POSHAN PEHL, SAMAR), but how far they reach into Murhu has not been mapped. [S25, S26]
objective: Within 24 months, improve dietary diversity and maternal and young-child feeding and care practices, and raise the uptake of ICDS and health services, among about 1,200 women from SHG member households with pregnant or lactating women and children under five in 20 villages of Murhu block, Khunti. All delivery runs through existing SHGs and government platforms.

results.impact: Contribution to improved nutritional status of mothers and children under five in tribal SHG households of Murhu block, Khunti.
outcomes: O1: Target households eat more diverse diets year-round, drawing on nutri-kitchen gardens and local foods.
O2: Pregnant and lactating women and caregivers adopt recommended maternal nutrition and infant and young child feeding (IYCF) and care practices.
O3: Pregnant women, mothers and children under five take up ICDS and health entitlements more fully, and at-risk children are identified, referred and followed up.
outputs: OP1.1: About 1,200 households have established and are maintaining climate-resilient nutri-kitchen gardens with local crops, greens, millets and fruit saplings.
OP1.2: 20 village demonstration plots, placed at or near Anganwadi centres where feasible, and 20 SHG-run community seed banks are functional.
OP2.1: 40 SHG women are selected, trained and working as Community Nutrition Resource Persons (CNRPs).
OP2.2: Monthly group counselling, cooking demonstrations and home visits in the first 1,000 days are delivered in all 20 villages.
OP3.1: SHG meetings are linked to Anganwadi and VHSND calendars in all 20 villages, and households are supported with THR, ANC/PNC, immunisation and PMMVY/JSY documentation.
OP3.2: A community growth-tracking and referral pathway to Anganwadi, CHC and MTC is functional, including post-discharge follow-up.
OP3.3: Anganwadi Workers (AWWs), ASHAs and SHG leaders are jointly trained, and quarterly block convergence meetings with ICDS and health officials are institutionalised.

OP4: The household tracking system, baseline and endline surveys, and learning products are delivered. The seed banks, counselling cadre and convergence routines are handed over to Village Organisations and SHG federations.

strategy_facts: The approach combines three pathways through one platform. Food access comes from kitchen gardens, behaviour change from counselling, and service uptake from ICDS and health convergence. The existing SHGs and Village Organisations deliver all three, with no parallel groups, as the applicant requires.

The counselling model follows the evidence on women's groups in eastern India, labelled here as external and demonstrated potential rather than local fact. The Ekjut participatory learning and action (PLA) trial in tribal Jharkhand and Odisha worked through 244 women's groups with local women facilitators and cut neonatal mortality by 45% in its last two years. The same model has since been delivered through ASHAs, which supports embedding it in government platforms. [S13, S14, S15]

The UPAVAN trial in rural Odisha (external evidence) found that SHG-based nutrition-sensitive agriculture combined with nutrition behaviour change raised minimum dietary diversity in children and mothers compared with controls, and that participation mattered. This is why kitchen gardens are paired with CNRP counselling and household tracking. [S16, S17]

Realistic targeting: the UPAVAN protocol notes that PLA and agriculture interventions change knowledge and dietary diversity strongly but nutritional status only a little. The primary outcomes are therefore diets, practices and service uptake. Anthropometry is tracked at impact level as a contribution only. [S18]

The garden design builds on EcoKheti's climate-resilient agriculture model (70% adoption among 800 farmers): millets, indigenous greens, fruit saplings, greywater use and seed saving. Field evidence from Jharkhand is limited but notes land and water constraints, so plots are sized to available homestead land and water. Crop lists will be confirmed with KVK Khunti and through community food mapping, because agro-climatic data are a gap. [S19]

CONVERGENCE, Didi Badi Yojana (JSLPS Poshan Vatika): The project will map coverage with JSLPS Murhu before starting. Where households are already covered, it will add counselling and service linkage and will not supply duplicate kits. [S25, S26]
CONVERGENCE, Poshan Vatika at Anganwadi centres: Village demonstration plots will be placed at or near Anganwadi centres or on Gram Panchayat land, as Government of India guidance encourages. [S23]

CONVERGENCE, Poshan 2.0 / Saksham Anganwadi: The project helps families take up the six Anganwadi services. It supplements growth monitoring and does not replace it; data are reconciled with AWW registers. [S22]

CONVERGENCE, PMMVY and JSY: CNRPs help pregnant women get documents ready (Aadhaar, bank seeding, MCP card) before AWWs and ASHAs register them. PMMVY pays Rs 5,000 in two instalments for the first child and Rs 6,000 for a second child who is a girl. JSY is paid after institutional delivery. These benefits flow to families as convergence and are not project cost. [S24]

CONVERGENCE, MGNREGA: Garden fencing, water structures and labour are to be sought through MGNREGA works. ST households in forest areas are entitled to 50 extra days of work on top of the standard 100. The project budget covers only demonstration-plot fencing and water support. [S27]

CONVERGENCE, NHM and MTC: The project strengthens the link from Anganwadi SAM detection to the MTC and adds community follow-up after discharge, responding to poor recovery after MTC discharge in Jharkhand. The status of SAMAR and POSHAN PEHL in Khunti will be checked and aligned with. [S12, S20, S25]
The project builds on EcoKheti's earlier SRLM-funded SHG nutrition work in Khunti and its FPO experience. Whether the target villages overlap with that earlier project area is still to be confirmed.

Sustainability: Village Organisations own the seed banks. CNRPs are linked to SHG federations and, where possible, to JSLPS cadres. Convergence routines are embedded in VHSND and block meetings by the end of the project.

risks.risk: Duplication with or crowding by JSLPS Didi Badi / FNHW interventions or existing cadres in the target villages
risks.mitigation: Map coverage with the JSLPS Murhu Block Mission Management Unit in Q1. Choose villages or households to complement existing coverage. Formalise roles in writing, and redirect kit budget to counselling and convergence where gardens already exist.

risks.risk: Dry spells, erratic monsoon or limited water and homestead land reduce the year-round viability of gardens
risks.mitigation: Use drought-tolerant indigenous crops and millets, greywater use, mulching and staggered sowing. Take advice from KVK Khunti. Seek MGNREGA water works, and size plots to the water available.
Use live fencing and local materials. Fence demonstration plots from project funds, and seek household fencing through MGNREGA convergence.

risks.risk: Weak Anganwadi or health service supply (THR irregularity, AWW or ASHA vacancies, VHSND not held) limits service uptake outcomes
risks.mitigation: Map service gaps in Q1. Raise supply issues at quarterly block and half-yearly district convergence meetings. Support VHSND through SHG participation. Track service availability separately from demand-side uptake.

risks.risk: No formal working relationship yet with the ICDS project office (CDPO), block health team or JSLPS
risks.mitigation: Seek letters of support or an MoU with the Murhu CDPO, the Medical Officer in charge of the CHC and the JSLPS Block Project Manager in the inception quarter. Use EcoKheti's existing SRLM relationship in Khunti.

risks.risk: CNRP drop-out because the honorarium is modest or domestic workload is heavy
risks.mitigation: Select CNRPs through SHGs with Village Organisation endorsement. Train two CNRPs per village for redundancy. Give recognition through the federation. Confirm the honorarium against the JSLPS CRP norm.

risks.risk: Remote villages and poor road connectivity or access conditions disrupt field presence and referral
risks.mitigation: Assess access and connectivity before selecting villages. Base each field facilitator in a cluster. Plan referrals using JSY/NHM transport, with a contingency fund.

risks.risk: Nutritional status changes are small or slow within 24 months, so the project appears to underperform
risks.mitigation: Set diets, practices and service uptake as the primary outcomes, as the evidence recommends. Present anthropometry as a contribution-level impact indicator only.

risks.risk: The indicative budget or target definition changes after donor engagement
risks.mitigation: The budget is modular (kits, CNRP numbers, surveys) and can be scaled. Confirm the target definition in the inception period.

activities_facts: A1 Inception and mobilisation (Q1): select and name the 20 villages; map SHGs, Village Organisations, JSLPS coverage, Anganwadi centres, ASHAs, VHSND and the nearest MTC; orient the SHGs and Village Organisations; identify pregnant and lactating women and children under five; secure support letters or MoUs with the CDPO, block health team and JSLPS.
A2 Baseline survey (Q1–Q2): measure household dietary diversity, maternal and child MDD, IYCF practices, service uptake (ANC, THR, immunisation, PMMVY), food security and anthropometry in the sample.
A3 Village nutrition action plans: SHGs develop and own a plan in each of the 20 villages through a participatory learning cycle.

A4 Nutri-kitchen gardens: run 40 one-day household training batches of 30 participants each; supply seed kits for 2 seasons to about 1,200 households and one set of 5 fruit saplings each; provide seasonal follow-up by the Kitchen Garden Specialist and CNRPs at the demonstration plots.

A5 Demonstration plots and seed banks: set up 20 plots at or near Anganwadi centres or on Gram Panchayat land, with fencing and low-cost water management, plus 20 community seed banks run by Village Organisations. Year-2 seed comes from these banks.

A6 Community Nutrition Resource Persons: select 40 CNRPs (2 per village) through SHGs; run 6 residential modules (3 batches × 2) and 6 non-residential refresher days each; equip them with pictorial counselling kits in the local language.

A7 Counselling delivery: hold monthly group sessions in SHG meetings; run 440 cooking demonstrations with local foods (1 per village per month for 22 months); make targeted home visits in pregnancy, lactation and the first 1,000 days; give households pictorial cards.
A8 ICDS and health convergence: align SHG meetings with Anganwadi and VHSND calendars; help families get THR, ANC/PNC, immunisation and PMMVY/JSY documents ready; support SHG participation in VHSND.

A9 Early identification and referral: supply supplementary growth-monitoring kits (one per village) used alongside the AWW; track at-risk mothers and children; refer SAM children to the MTC; follow up children after discharge together with the AWW.

A10 Frontline capacity building: hold 8 joint AWW, ASHA and SHG leader training batches (4 rounds); run 2 in-state exposure visits for 60 leaders and CNRPs; hold 8 quarterly block and 4 half-yearly district convergence meetings.

A11 Monitoring, evaluation and learning: run a mobile household tracking system on 24 devices; hold quarterly reviews with SHG federations and block officials; run the endline survey (Q8); produce case studies and learning briefs.
A12 Sustainability and handover (Q7–Q8): transfer seed banks to Village Organisations, link CNRPs to federations and JSLPS cadres, and record convergence routines in block meeting minutes.

budget_adjustments: The first full build came to about Rs 1.52 Crore including overheads, so it was trimmed to fit the Rs 1.4 Crore ceiling while keeping the core delivery model: 40 CNRPs, gardens for all 1,200 households, convergence and both surveys.
Household kitchen garden training was cut from 2 days to 1 day per batch (Rs 9,60,000 to Rs 4,80,000). Seasonal refreshers move to the demonstration plots and SHG meetings at no extra cost.
Purchased seed kits were cut from 3 seasons to 2 (Year 1), with Year-2 seed from the community seed banks. This reinforces sustainability and saves about Rs 2.4 lakh.
The field facilitator estimate was set at Rs 18,000 rather than Rs 20,000 per month, saving Rs 1,92,000.
The survey rounds were costed at Rs 3,50,000 each rather than Rs 4,00,000, with a smaller sample.
The documentation lump sum was reduced from Rs 2,00,000 to Rs 1,50,000, and the mobile data rate from Rs 200 to Rs 150 per device-month.
CNRP honoraria are costed for months 3–24 (22 months), after selection and initial training.
Overheads were set at 7% of direct costs so the total fits the ceiling. If the donor allows a higher rate, some estimated programme lines will need rebalancing.

Household fencing and water structures are not in the budget. They are to be sought through MGNREGA and Didi Badi convergence. PMMVY and JSY benefits reach families as convergence and are not project cost.

flags: BUDGET: Rs 1.4 Crore is an indicative planning envelope, not a figure given by the applicant or a donor. It must be confirmed. 20 of the 31 budget lines are estimates and are listed in rates_to_confirm.

SALARY NORMS: The JSLPS salary band dates from 2019 and was found on a third-party site. No escalation to 2026-28 has been applied. Verify against the current JSLPS schedule; any escalation will need rebalancing within the ceiling.

TARGET DEFINITION: It is not yet clear whether the ~1,200 women are all pregnant or lactating women, or SHG member women of whom those groups form a subset. The number of children under five is unknown and will be established at baseline.
VILLAGES: The 20 villages are not yet named. Overlap with EcoKheti's earlier Khunti project area and with JSLPS Didi Badi or FNHW coverage is unconfirmed, and there is a duplication risk.

DATA GAP: Khunti's NFHS-5 district fact-sheet values were not retrieved. The problem analysis uses Jharkhand state values, which are labelled as state-level. Project-area values will come from the baseline.

SECONDARY SOURCES: The Murhu block Census figures, district tribal composition, Khunti BPL share and NFHS-4 district ranking come from secondary compilations (Wikipedia, CSO forum). Verify them against the DCHB and official fact sheets before submission.
CONFLICT: The Khunti sex ratio is given as 997 (district website) and as 994 (other compilations). It is not used in the proposal until resolved from the DCHB.

UNKNOWN LOCAL SYSTEMS: The number of Anganwadi centres in Murhu, AWW and ASHA vacancies, VHSND functioning, the nearest MTC, the status of SAMAR and POSHAN PEHL, and any Jharkhand ICDS–NHM–JSLPS convergence order are all unknown. They are to be mapped in Q1.
PARTNERSHIPS: No existing MoU or working relationship with the Murhu CDPO, block health team or JSLPS has been confirmed.
ACCESS: Village connectivity and security or access conditions in Murhu are unverified and need a field assessment.
AGRO-CLIMATE: Rainfall, soil, water and local crop suitability data for Khunti are gaps. Crop lists will be confirmed with KVK Khunti and through community food mapping.

EXTERNAL EVIDENCE: The Ekjut, UPAVAN (Odisha) and Dungarpur (Rajasthan) evidence is used as demonstrated potential only, not as local fact. Logframe targets are project aspirations set relative to a baseline that has not yet been measured.
